name: Hardware Startup

claims.claim_text: The structural advantage of hardware over software is defensibility through time. A software product can be displaced within a month by someone smarter writing a better one, whereas a product that took six to twelve months to develop is not easily knocked off its position.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone's not going to come along easily and knock you off your perch
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: The counter-argument from an accelerator that funds both: at the earliest stages, ignoring per-unit cost as you should, nothing in hardware need take more than about a week longer than the software equivalent, whether that is populated boards or a printed enclosure.
claims.quote_verbatim: It shouldn't take you more than a week longer to do any aspect of your project at the earliest stages
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Hardware carries one structural advantage that is easy to overlook: people expect to pay for it. Building a business on something customers already accept they must buy removes a problem software companies spend years solving.
claims.quote_verbatim: people expect to pay for hardware, unlike software
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: What the phrase hardware is hard actually refers to is two specific absences: there is no built-in distribution channel comparable to an application store reaching millions of users instantly, and there is no recompiling, because manufacturing has to physically happen.
claims.quote_verbatim: There is no recompiling hardware
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: The historical reason hardware was underfunded is margin. Selling a widget at twenty or thirty points of gross margin is a genuinely hard business, so both investors and experienced founders were cautious about it, and the sector underperformed as a result.
claims.quote_verbatim: selling a widget for, you know, 20, 30 points of, of, of gross margin dollars
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: What changed was the definition rather than the economics. Hardware stopped being a widget that sits in a house collecting dust and became the mechanism for putting software into someone's life away from a screen, which is what made it investable again.
claims.quote_verbatim: hardware being a really good mechanism of getting software into a user's life in a way that's not on a screen
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: From an investor's side the difficulty is concrete: within the first fifteen employees a hardware company often has to cover eight, nine or ten distinct disciplines that must work together effectively, which is a coordination problem a software company does not have.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the first 15 employees, you often can represent eight, nine, 10 distinct disciplines
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The difference also shows up in the accounts. A hardware company has a cost of goods sold, so the profit and loss statement contains materials as well as people, which changes every financial conversation about the business.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not just people anymore. It's stuff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The falling-component-cost effect that produced the smartphone era is now running in robotics: motor controllers, battery technology and laser rangefinders have all dropped far enough to open markets that were previously priced out entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: Think about how much LIDAR used to cost
claims.speaker: Eric Klein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric Klein

claims.claim_text: The full inventory of what a hardware company must do explains the difficulty: a product and a platform, software and electrical and mechanical engineering, new product introduction, contract manufacturers, then distribution, supply chain, logistics and multiple compliance certifications.
claims.quote_verbatim: the triple black diamond of entrepreneurship
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: A successful crowdfunding campaign is the beginning of the risk rather than the end of it. Founders who have raised a few hundred thousand often believe they are through the difficult part, when the difficult part has not started.
claims.quote_verbatim: they're just starting the risk level
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Avidan Ross

claims.claim_text: The cost asymmetry stated concretely: a software company's costs are chairs, computers, snacks and people. A hardware company adds tooling that can run to six figures, prototype boards that cost thousands to get quickly, and regulatory approvals.
claims.quote_verbatim: a hardware startup has to be like, oh, and also $100,000 in molds
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: The advice that follows from that breadth is to identify and accept your weaknesses and buy in help for them. Specialised areas such as antenna design are where a general hardware team will otherwise lose months.
claims.quote_verbatim: identify and accept your weaknesses and get help
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Omer Kilic

claims.claim_text: There are three viable scales and the middle one is the trap. Small one-off projects work, and a very large raise lets you hire a team, but in between you have neither the money to hire people nor the option to ignore the work, so you do everything yourself continuously.
claims.quote_verbatim: the pit of despair
claims.episode_title: Ceramic capacitors & High end scopes - Kempt Kickstarter Kakorrhaphiophobia

claims.claim_text: The case for bootstrapping rests on the actual numbers: unless you are doing something unusually expensive, hardware development runs to thousands rather than hundreds of thousands, which is within reach of a few years of saving.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're only talking thousands
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Gnomic Gazumping Gobemouche

claims.claim_text: The limit of bootstrapping is scale rather than survival. An order-of-magnitude jump in production capacity, such as moving from a small facility to one ten times the size, comes from investment because the margin on the existing product cannot fund it.
claims.quote_verbatim: that continual bootstrapping thing doesn't get you, you know, that order of magnitude gain
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Investor appetite is narrower than the opportunity. The money goes to consumer gadgets rather than heavy machinery, even where the unglamorous market is demonstrably large, because one is fundable and the other is not.
claims.quote_verbatim: they don't want tractors. They want gadgets
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: The semiconductor version of that constraint: everyone starts without their own production, because even venture funding only covers the designers, the tools and the licences. Owning production comes decades later out of revenue, if at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: they all start fabless
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: The cash-heaviness becomes concrete at product level. One company's pre-sales target determined whether it could continue at all, against non-recurring engineering costs running into millions for a single custom display.
claims.quote_verbatim: just to the NRE, just for that display is $4 million
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: A category of mistakes is unavoidable rather than careless: choosing the wrong corporate structure, misclassifying goods for tariffs, discovering compliance obligations late. The realistic posture is to expect them, pay the penalties and keep learning rather than to plan them away.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't know what you didn't know in the beginning
claims.speaker: Christina Cyr
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Christina Cyr

claims.claim_text: Every hardware startup needs someone in the role of reality bringer, insisting that fourteen-week lead-time parts be ordered now. That person is generally treated as difficult, because startups are structurally reactive and the deadline does not feel real yet.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're the, you're the reality bringer
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: The underlying reason that conflict exists is cash timing. The software model is cash light while hardware is cash heavy, so committing money to parts months ahead of revenue runs against how the rest of the company is operating.
claims.quote_verbatim: the software model is so like cash light and hardware is so cash heavy
claims.episode_title: Cellular IoT with Jared Wolff

claims.claim_text: A manufacturing consultancy's core customers build between five thousand and a million units, but the companies that reach that scale usually start far below it, frequently after false starts and financing that fell through.
claims.quote_verbatim: typically looking to build between 5,000 and a million units
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller (2nd)

claims.claim_text: What is sobering about the successful ones is how ordinary they looked early. A brilliant team and an interesting product did not distinguish them from a hundred other startups with the same characteristics; the traction came later and was not predictable from the starting position.
claims.quote_verbatim: there wasn't anything that distinguished them from the other a hundred or so startups
claims.speaker: Scott Miller
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Miller (2nd)

claims.claim_text: An accelerator application is worth completing even if you never submit it, because the questions are ones a founder should be asking anyway: how you will make money, how equity is divided, and what you understand about the market that competitors do not.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's really questions you should be asking yourself anyways
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: The terms of one well-known programme: roughly twenty thousand dollars for about seven percent of the company, founders present for a three-month batch, with as much or as little help as they choose to seek. Some companies extract very little from it.
claims.quote_verbatim: essentially $20,000 for what boils down to basically 7% of your company
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: Reapplying after rejection with visible progress is read as a positive signal rather than a negative one, because it identifies a team that is executing regardless of whether the investor participates.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting rejected, showing progress and applying again
claims.speaker: Luke Iseman
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Luke Iseman of yCombinator

claims.claim_text: What an accelerator is not is a source of hardware expertise. Going to one expecting to be taught how to build hardware is a misunderstanding of what is on offer; what they can help with is scaling a company.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't go to Y Combinator for them to teach you about hardware
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: The startup advice itself does not change by domain: build something people want, find a way to distribute it, find a way to market it, sell it. Hardware and software differ in execution rather than in what the business has to achieve.
claims.quote_verbatim: Build something that people want, find a way to distribute it
claims.episode_title: Interview with the Upverter Founders - Ramiform Reciprocity Raconteurs

claims.claim_text: Successful hardware founders overwhelmingly have prior industry experience rather than coming directly from education, which is a different pattern from software and reflects how much of the difficulty is operational rather than technical.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of them have some sort of industry experience
claims.episode_title: Prior Art, Wafer Fabs and Guns - Whimsical Wafer Waffling

claims.claim_text: The visible record is heavily distorted by survivorship. You hear about the successes and almost nothing about the failures, while the proportion of startups that produce a genuinely useful product and succeed is very small.
claims.quote_verbatim: you only hear about the successes. You don't hear about the failures
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: The scale of that invisibility is worth stating: on one practitioner's estimate ninety-nine percent of hardware startups go under the radar entirely, so the sample anyone reasons from is the visible one percent.
claims.quote_verbatim: 99% of them go under the radar
claims.episode_title: Standing With Ahmed

claims.claim_text: A specific and underestimated gap is purchasing. A new hardware company generally knows nothing about the mechanics of buying components, which is precisely where an inexperienced buyer gets poor terms on a reel of parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: how many hardware startups know, like purchasing the ins and outs of purchasing
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: A blunt readiness test: if nobody in the company knows what design for manufacture means, a hardware startup is probably the wrong idea, because getting something manufactured is the difficult part rather than designing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing a hardware startup is probably not the best idea
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dr Greg Charvat - Watcher of Wraithlike Walls

claims.claim_text: Pricing is not the bill of materials plus a percentage. Taking the component cost and adding twenty percent for margin does not work, and margin calculation is its own discipline that founders routinely underestimate.
claims.quote_verbatim: you look at your bomb cost and then I'll add 20% or something for your margin and that just doesn't work that way
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jon Oxer - Innoxious Implant Innovator

claims.claim_text: Easy money is a warning rather than an opportunity. When capital becomes readily available everyone enters the space, which indicates a phase in the funding cycle rather than durable demand for what is being built.
claims.quote_verbatim: Money is too easy to get
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: B Plus Boards and D Minus Cities - Uneath Urban Ubication

claims.claim_text: The corresponding question nobody asks during a boom is what happens to those companies when interest cools again, since the capital that made them viable is the thing most likely to disappear.
claims.quote_verbatim: when hardware goes cold again
claims.episode_title: Questioning Everyday Prototyping - Verrucose Vehicle Vitilitigation

claims.claim_text: That cooling did arrive. The boom period ended, fewer people start hardware companies now, and of those starting companies at all more go into software or financial technology, which is worth knowing when reading advice written during the peak.
claims.quote_verbatim: now that's cooled off a lot
claims.episode_title: Finishing Prototypes with Zack Freedman

claims.claim_text: A structural recruiting disadvantage: hardware companies are tied to physical locations, so an engineer's employment options are limited to companies within reach of where they live, while a software engineer can in principle work from anywhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: hardware companies are locked to locations
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: The hardware community stays small through selection rather than through lack of awareness. The work is hard and the comparative payout in software is better, so most people who could do it choose not to.
claims.quote_verbatim: most people just aren't really interested in doing it
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Cousins

claims.claim_text: An honest inventory from a founder returning to the field: listing everything he loved and did not love about running a consumer hardware company produced a much longer list of dislikes. That exercise is what makes deliberately narrowing the scope of the next attempt attractive.
claims.quote_verbatim: The list of things that I didn't like was much longer than the things that I did like
claims.speaker: Eric Migicovsky
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: One viable category is the product that can be cloned easily but survives on brand rather than on technical defensibility, which requires a different funding profile from a product protected by its difficulty.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's something that can be cloned really easily, but it is more of a brand
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: The gap worth noticing is between what people need and what gets built. Affordable transportation and cheaper energy are hardware problems people genuinely have, and almost nobody starts a company to address them, because the practical work is unglamorous.
claims.quote_verbatim: so many things that people need in their lives that are hardware related and no startup is doing it
claims.episode_title: Don't Turn It On, Don't Take It Apart
